title: The Centre-state divide in food safety regulation
syllabus: GS2 › Functions and responsibilities of the Union and the States; issues in the federal structure · GS2 › Statutory, regulatory and quasi-judicial bodies · GS2 › Issues relating to health · GS4 › Good governance
summary: Maharashtra has gone to the Bombay High Court alleging that the national regulator FSSAI created a parallel enforcement mechanism and encroached on the state's powers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
ideas: Act gives enforcement to states; FSSAI sets standards and licenses big firms.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
National standards, local enforcement.
FSSAI's central inspectors and wider licensing seen as a parallel mechanism.
GS2 · Federal friction
Regulators can redraw federalism by executive order.
Rules changed without public consultation weaken legitimacy.
GS2 · Rule of law / GS4 · Transparency
Process matters as much as purpose.
keywords: A central body duplicating enforcement that a law gives to states
A parallel regulatory mechanism breeds turf wars and confuses businesses about whom to answer to.
Rules and orders made by an executive body under powers given by a statute
Delegated legislation must stay within the parent Act; orders creating central FSOs test that limit.
How regulatory powers are shared between national and state authorities
Food safety is a test of regulatory federalism: national standards, local enforcement.
Outcomes that rest on one officer's leadership rather than systems
A central official asked whether Maharashtra's good enforcement would survive one officer's transfer: institutions must outlast individuals.
examples: GST Council: Centre and states decide together.
FSSAI and states acting on one food safety scare
Maggi ban, 2015: FSSAI and states acting on one food safety scare.
Pre-legislative consultation: public comment before rules.
pyqs: Recent changes in Centre-State relations; building trust.
National parties' centralisation vs regional parties' autonomy.
CBI jurisdiction in states; withholding consent.
CCI curbing abuse of dominance by MNCs.
State's role in containing marketisation of public healthcare.

trend.t: Centre–state questions have moved from constitutional devices (Article 356, 2023; Governors, 2022 and 2026) to everyday friction in shared domains: CBI consent (2021), building trust (2024) and fiscal federalism (2025). Regulatory bodies are asked one at a time (CCI 2023, tribunals 2025).
trend.watch: Centre–state relations have been asked every year from 2021 to 2026, increasingly through concrete disputes, so a regulator–state turf war like FSSAI is the kind of example UPSC now rewards.
focus: Concurrent-list domains: health, food, police cooperation
Delegated legislation and limits of regulators

potential: "Regulatory bodies are becoming a new site of Centre–state friction." Examine with reference to food safety regulation in India. (10 marks)
Discuss how cooperative federalism can be strengthened in regulatory domains shared by the Union and the States. (15 marks)

practice.q: "Regulatory bodies are becoming a new site of Centre–state friction." Examine with reference to food safety regulation in India.
parts: The case for a central role

answer.t: In 2026 Maharashtra moved the Bombay High Court alleging that FSSAI had built a 'parallel enforcement mechanism' that encroaches on state powers under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.

pts.t: Regulators expand roles through orders rather than amendments.
pts.ex: FSSAI's May 2023 order creating central FSOs, though the Act vests appointment in state Commissioners.

pts.t: Central licensing widened to new categories.
pts.ex: E-commerce platforms, five-star hotels, nutraceuticals and proprietary foods.

pts.t: Rules changed without consultation erode trust.
pts.ex: March 2026 threshold change from Rs 20 crore to Rs 50 crore without public consultation.

pts.t: States inspect but must report to the central authority, which runs proceedings.
pts.ex: Reports from state officers go to the central licensing authority.

answer.h: The case for a central role

pts.t: Enforcement varies across states and over time.
pts.ex: A central official's concern that one state's record depends on one officer.

pts.t: Inter-state and export businesses need one standard.
pts.ex: Central licence for businesses operating across state lines.

pts.t: If central enforcement is needed, Parliament should amend the Act.
Shared inspection protocols and data between FSSAI and state commissioners.
pts.ex: A food safety council on the GST Council model.

pts.t: Mandatory public and state consultation before rule changes.

answer.t: Food safety needs one standard and many hands: national rules enforced locally, with states treated as partners, not subordinates.

title: Karnataka widens ethanol probe to distribution network, CM slams Centre
syllabus: GS3 › Infrastructure: energy; biofuels · GS2 › Issues in the federal structure · GS2 › Consumer protection (governance)
summary: Karnataka's probe into alleged excess ethanol blending in petrol has moved from pumps to blending and distribution agencies after lab tests found up to 31.2% ethanol against the E20 (20%) limit.
ideas: Over-blending (up to 31.2% vs E20) hurts vehicles; consumers pay.
GS3 · Biofuels
Targets need quality control.
Standards are central, complaints are local: needs joint enforcement.
GS2 · Centre–state
Shared domains need shared accountability.
keywords: Petrol with 20% ethanol, the prescribed blend
E20 is India's blending benchmark; samples at 30% show why monitoring must keep pace with targets.
Certification of testing laboratories for reliable results
NABL-accredited testing gives a state's findings evidentiary weight against large oil companies.
examples: Ethanol % displayed at the pump: transparency for the consumer.
pyqs: Energy independence by 2047 through clean technology.
Recent changes in Centre-State relations; building trust.

trend.t: Energy questions moved from renewables targets (2022) to energy independence by 2047 (2025) and energy security challenges (2026); biofuels sit within this as an import-substitution tool.
trend.watch: Energy security was asked in 2025 and 2026, so the trade-offs of each tool, including ethanol blending's costs for consumers and food crops, are worth preparing.

potential: Ethanol blending serves India's energy security but raises concerns for consumers and food security. Discuss. (10 marks)

title: Flagship fest ahead, why Nagaland wants permit regime scrapped
syllabus: GS3 › Security challenges and their management in border areas; Linkages of development and security · GS2 › Federalism and Centre–state relations; Issues relating to the Northeast · GS1 › Tribal culture · GS4 › Citizen-friendly administration
summary: Nagaland has urged the Centre to completely withdraw the Protected Area Permit for foreigners, reimposed in December 2024 for security reasons, saying it hurts tourism ahead of the Hornbill Festival.
ideas: Two permits, two purposes: the PAP (Foreigners (Protected Areas) Order, 1958) controls foreigners' entry to border states, while the colonial-era ILP regulates Indian citizens to protect indigenous hill cultures.
GS3 · Border management / GS1 · Tribal culture
India's permit regimes serve two aims: security at the border (PAP) and protection of tribal cultures (ILP).
Security versus development: relaxed in 2011 and reimposed in December 2024 for security reasons, the PAP now clashes with the state's push for tourism and investment.
GS3 · Linkages of security and development
In peaceful border states, rigid security rules can choke the development that itself secures the region.
A rule from another era: the CM argues that a regulation designed for a different security environment should not hold back a peaceful state's aspirations.
GS2 · Governance / Policy review
Rules must be reviewed as conditions change; regulations that outlive their purpose become obstacles.
Process matters as much as policy: bureaucracy, a convoluted application process and last-minute relaxations deter foreign tourists who plan months ahead.
GS2 · Governance / GS4 · Citizen-friendly administration
Predictable, simple procedures matter as much as the rule itself for tourism and trust.
Federal voice: the state wants a central rule changed and has taken it to the Union Home Minister, but awaits a decision.
GS2 · Federalism
Nagaland's appeal on the PAP shows states seeking a voice in central rules that shape their development.
keywords: Central permit for foreigners to visit designated border areas
The PAP balances border security against openness to foreign visitors.
Permit for Indian citizens to enter certain northeastern states
The ILP protects indigenous cultures from demographic and economic pressures.
The idea that development and security reinforce each other
In the Northeast, tourism-led development can strengthen peace as much as security controls.
Reviewing or ending a rule once its purpose has passed
A sunset review would test whether the PAP still serves security in peaceful states.
Tourism built on a region's living culture and festivals
Festivals like Hornbill turn culture into livelihoods and soft power.
examples: Flagship festival drawing visitors from across the world
GS1 · Culture · GS3 · Tourism · Act East
The Hornbill Festival is an example of the Northeast's cultural soft power and tourism potential.
Security rule swinging with the security assessment
The PAP's relaxation and reimposition show security policy shifting with threat perceptions.
Relaxation announced only around the festival gives tourists no certainty
A relaxation that comes too late to plan for is an example of form over substance in administration.
pyqs: Internal security challenges and peace accords in the North-Eastern States.
Security challenges in policing the border in North-East India beyond insurgency.
Border Area Development Programmes and civic action in Ladakh.
Challenges and strategies for effective border management.
Hill states reaching the limits of ecological carrying capacity due to tourism.

trend.t: Northeast questions moved from insurgency and border policing (2017, 2019) to peace accords (2025), while border questions shifted in 2026 to development programmes that win hearts and minds. The direction is from security alone to security through development.
trend.watch: The Northeast and border management are asked almost every year. Prepare the balance of security and development, peace processes and border-area development.
focus: Security and development in border areas
Northeast: peace processes and special arrangements
Permit regimes (PAP, ILP) and tribal protection
Tourism and the Act East policy

Examine the potential of cultural tourism in the economic development of the Northeast. (10 marks)

practice.q: "In India's border states, development is itself a security strategy." Discuss with reference to the Northeast.

answer.t: In November 2026 Nagaland asked the Centre to withdraw the Protected Area Permit, reimposed in 2024, arguing that a rule from another security era holds back a peaceful state's development.

pts.t: Livelihoods cut the pool of youth drawn to insurgency.
Visitors bring income and integrate the region with the world.
pts.ex: Hornbill Festival draws visitors from many countries.

pts.t: Roads, rail and air links bind border areas to the mainland.
Schools, health and services build trust in government.
Thriving villages deter infiltration better than empty borders.
Development sustains peace accords.
pts.ex: Peace accords in the Northeast in the past decade.

pts.t: Movement of insurgents, arms and drugs across international borders.
Instability in Myanmar affects the region.
Proximity to China calls for caution on foreign access.
The ILP shields indigenous identity from outside pressure.
Relax the PAP where conditions are peaceful, with safeguards.
Online, time-bound approvals that foreigners can plan for.
Involve states in decisions on central rules that shape their economies.
Technology at borders so that security does not depend on blanket restrictions.
Tourism, crafts and agro-processing for local youth.
Community-led tourism that respects indigenous ways of life.

answer.t: In the Northeast, a confident state secures its borders by opening its doors with care; balancing permits with prosperity is the surest path to lasting peace.

title: Andhra braces for landfall, rescue teams mobilised in Odisha as Murasu approaches
syllabus: GS3 › Disaster and disaster management · GS2 › Federalism: inter-state cooperation · GS1 › Cyclones · GS4 › Empathy and compassion
summary: Days after Cyclone Arnab, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha prepared for Cyclone Murasu; Tamil Nadu sent 500 electricity staff to help Andhra restore power.
evolution: Cyclone Arnab's rains cause landslides in Odisha; 300 villages marooned in Ganjam (page 11).
Andhra braces for a second cyclone, Murasu (page 7).
Murasu nears landfall; Tamil Nadu sends power crews to Andhra.
ideas: Back-to-back cyclones: less than a week after Arnab, a severe cyclonic storm forced a second round of evacuations and school closures in Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.
GS1 · Cyclones / GS3 · Disaster management
Back-to-back cyclones test whether preparedness can be sustained, not just mounted once.
States help states: at Andhra's request, Tamil Nadu deployed 500 electricity department personnel in 25 teams to restore power.
GS2 · Cooperative federalism
Tamil Nadu's power crews for Andhra show cooperative federalism working horizontally, state to state.
Turning a hazard into a resource: Andhra's CM asked officials to use the heavy rainfall to fill tanks and reservoirs through efficient water management, and to finish restoration within 48 hours.
GS3 · Water management / DM
Linking flood response with reservoir filling turns a disaster into water security.
Impact beyond landfall: though landfall was in Andhra, Odisha's southern districts were put on high alert and evacuations prioritised.
GS3 · Disaster preparedness
Cyclone preparedness must cover neighbouring regions, not just the landfall zone.
keywords: Inter-state help in disasters is horizontal federalism in action.
States lending personnel and equipment in emergencies
Mutual-aid arrangements speed up restoration after disasters.
Time target to restore essential services
A 48-hour restoration target keeps recovery accountable.
data: Wind speed of Severe Cyclonic Storm Murasu at landfall
Murasu crossed the Andhra coast as a severe cyclonic storm with winds of 100–110 km/h (IMD).

Tamil Nadu sent 500 electricity staff in 25 teams to restore power in cyclone-hit Andhra.
examples: Tamil Nadu's power crews for Andhra
One state's workers restoring another state's grid after a cyclone
GS2 · Cooperative federalism · GS3 · Disaster management · GS4 · Empathy beyond borders
Tamil Nadu's crews in Andhra show empathy crossing state lines, the human face of cooperative federalism.
Using cyclone rainfall to fill tanks and reservoirs
GS3 · Water management · GS3 · Disaster management
Andhra's plan to fill reservoirs from cyclone rain shows disasters can be managed for long-term gain.
pyqs: Colour-coded weather warnings for cyclone-prone areas.
Sea surface temperature rise and tropical cyclones.
Disaster resilience and the Sendai Framework.
Building trust between the Centre and the States.
potential: "Disasters reveal the strength of cooperative federalism in India." Discuss with recent examples. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Disasters reveal the strength of cooperative federalism in India." Discuss with recent examples.

answer.t: As Cyclone Murasu hit Andhra Pradesh days after Cyclone Arnab, Tamil Nadu sent 500 electricity staff in 25 teams to restore its neighbour's power.

pts.t: States lend personnel and equipment.
pts.ex: Tamil Nadu's power crews in Andhra.

pts.t: NDRF, armed forces and disaster funds.
IMD alerts reach all coastal states.
Neighbouring states prepare together.
Help depends on requests, not standing pacts.
Centre–state rows over relief funds.
Uneven state disaster forces.
Pre-agreed inter-state support.
Coastal states plan jointly.

answer.t: When a cyclone crosses a coastline, it erases state borders; India's federalism is strongest when its states respond as one.
